records.why: Lesson 3 asks for an ammeter practical at four points in series, a parallel demonstration, I = Q/t calculations, a CER statement, the Driving Question Board and a model revision. That cannot fit 40 minutes, and the old text itself recommended a double lesson. The teacher must decide: keep it as one 80-minute double period (suggested) or keep 40 minutes and make the parallel readings a teacher demonstration only.
records.old: 40 minutes (double lesson of 80 minutes recommended if the practical is done by every group)
records.new: 80 minutes (2 x 40-minute periods)
records.group_headline: Four lessons (3, 7, 9, 11) held a full practical plus calculations and could not fit 40 minutes: now 80-minute double periods. Unit total recomputed (880 min = 22 periods, matching KICD's 22 lessons); lessons 4, 10 and 12 get minute-by-minute pacing.

records.why: Lesson 7 has 12 meter readings, a derivation, power calculations, a CER write-up, Driving Question Board and model in one period. The old text already said a double period 'may be used'. Now 80 minutes. Knock-on of the Lesson 3 timing fix.
records.old: 40 minutes (one double period may be used if the bench measurements run long)
records.new: 80 minutes (2 x 40-minute periods)

records.why: Lesson 9 builds and measures a mixed circuit, compares cells, reduces the circuit on whiteboards, then does Driving Question Board and model work. The Observe phase is a bench build, so the 'single lesson' option could not work. Now 80 minutes. Knock-on of the Lesson 3 timing fix.
records.old: 40 minutes (single lesson; extend to a double lesson of 80 minutes if students build the mixed circuit on the bench)
records.new: 80 minutes (2 x 40-minute periods)

records.why: Lesson 11 has a calculation task, a low-voltage fuse demonstration, three inspection stations, a CER write-up, Driving Question Board and a model. The old text recommended a double lesson. Now 80 minutes. Knock-on of the Lesson 3 timing fix.
records.old: 40 minutes (one double lesson of 2 x 40 minutes recommended if the fuse demonstration is performed)
records.new: 80 minutes (2 x 40-minute periods)

records.why: Lesson 10 stays a single 40-minute period. The cost task is paper-based, and the pacing note now added to the Predict phase shows how it fits. The 'double lesson may be used' option is removed so the duration is unambiguous. Knock-on of the Lesson 3 timing fix.
records.old: 40 minutes (one double lesson of 80 minutes may be used for the full cost task)
records.new: 40 minutes (single period; the cost task is paper-based, see the pacing note in the Predict phase)

records.why: Recomputed from each lesson's real duration: Lessons 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 are 80 minutes (10 x 80 = 800) and Lessons 4 and 10 are 40 minutes (2 x 40 = 80), so 800 + 80 = 880 minutes = 22 periods of 40 minutes. The old text said 12 x 40 = 480, which ignored the double periods. 22 periods also matches the 22 lessons KICD allocates to this sub-strand.
records.old: 12 lessons × 40 minutes = 480 minutes total
records.new: 12 lessons: 10 double lessons of 80 minutes and 2 single lessons of 40 minutes = 880 minutes in total (22 periods of 40 minutes)

records.why: Lesson 4 is a single 40-minute period with four voltmeter tasks, an explanation with calculations, the Driving Question Board and a model. Minute-by-minute pacing is added, and task 4 becomes a quick teacher demonstration if groups run short. Checked: with one series bulb removed the voltmeter (very high resistance) carries almost no current, so almost the whole 9 V appears across the gap and it reads about 9 V.
records.old: Say: 'Last lesson we saw 0.10 A at every point in the series loop.
records.new: Pacing for this 40-minute lesson: Predict 5 min, Observe 15 min (groups do tasks 1 to 3; task 4 is a quick teacher demonstration if groups run short: with one series bulb removed the voltmeter across the gap reads about 9 V, because almost all of the battery p.d. appears across the break), Explain 10 min, Driving Question Board 4 min, Model Building 6 min. Say: 'Last lesson we saw 0.10 A at every point in the series loop.

records.why: Lesson 10 is a single 40-minute period. Pacing added (5 + 10 + 15 + 4 + 6 = 40). Re-measuring the whole demo would take the whole period, so the Observe phase reuses the Lesson 7 and 8 readings and only re-checks one series bulb and one parallel bulb.
records.old: Reconnect both circuits.
records.new: Pacing for this 40-minute lesson: Predict 5 min, Observe 10 min (use the readings already recorded in Lessons 7 and 8 and only re-check one series bulb and one parallel bulb), Explain 15 min (paper calculations: the tubes first, then the bulb comparison), Driving Question Board 4 min, Model Building 6 min. Reconnect both circuits.

records.why: Lesson 12 packs a bench re-check, the Final Explanation, the Driving Question Board, a model comparison, a design task and a gallery walk into 80 minutes. Pacing added (8 + 17 + 20 + 10 + 25 = 80).
records.old: Display the Lesson 1 initial model posters and the DQB.
records.new: Pacing for this 80-minute lesson: Predict 8 min, Observe 17 min (one class data table), Explain 20 min, Driving Question Board 10 min, Model Building and design 25 min. Display the Lesson 1 initial model posters and the DQB.

records.why: Lesson 7 uses P = IV (0.30 W per bulb) and Lesson 8 uses it again, but power is only taught in Lesson 10, so learners were asked to use a formula they had not met. A one-minute link is added using what they already know: 1 V = 1 J/C (Lesson 4) and 1 A = 1 C/s (Lesson 3), so volts x amps = J/C x C/s = J/s. Lesson 10 still develops power, energy and cost in full.
records.old: Ask: "Compare 0.30 W with 2.7 W. How many times smaller is it?"
records.new: Before Step 4, give a one-minute link to power: "A watt is a joule per second. From Lesson 4, 1 V = 1 J per coulomb; from Lesson 3, 1 A = 1 coulomb per second. So volts x amps = joules per coulomb x coulombs per second = joules per second, which is P = IV. We use it here only to compare the bulbs, and Lesson 10 develops it fully with energy and cost." Ask: "Compare 0.30 W with 2.7 W. How many times smaller is it?"
records.group_headline: Power (P = IV) was used in Lessons 7 and 8 before it was taught in Lesson 10: Lesson 7 now gives a one-minute link from ideas learners already have.

records.why: Lesson 9 said Lesson 10 teaches P = IV, but Lesson 7 now introduces it briefly. Wording made consistent.
records.old: (L10 teaches P = IV)
records.new: (P = IV was introduced briefly in Lesson 7 and is developed in Lesson 10)

records.why: The Explain-phase problem told learners that the three bulbs 'were 90 Ω in total', which gives away the Lesson 7 discovery that series resistances add, and clashed with the Model phase, which still marks 90 Ω as 'to be tested in L7'. Now learners work out the total resistance of the loop from data they already have (9 V, 0.10 A). Recomputed: 9 / 0.10 = 90 ohm.
records.old: 'In the series loop the three bulbs were 90 Ω in total with a 9 V supply. Using V = IR, what current do you expect?' (I = 9/90 = 0.10 A, matching the measurement).
records.new: 'In the series loop the supply was 9 V and the measured current was 0.10 A. Using R = V/I, what is the total resistance of the loop?' (R = 9/0.10 = 90 Ω. We do not yet know how the three bulbs make up this 90 Ω, which is the question for Lesson 7).

records.why: At 7.5 V a 30 Ω resistor dissipates P = V^2/R = 7.5 x 7.5 / 30 = 1.875 W, about 1.9 W. A common 0.25 W or 0.5 W carbon resistor would overheat or burn out at the top readings (4.5 V already gives 0.675 W). The note tells teachers to use a wire-wound resistor of 2 W or more. Teachers should check what resistors their school has.
records.old: Open the switch between readings, because the resistor warms slightly if current flows for long.
records.new: Use a wire-wound 30 Ω resistor rated at 2 W or more: at 7.5 V it dissipates P = V²/R = 56.25/30 = about 1.9 W, which would overheat a common 0.25 W or 0.5 W carbon resistor. Open the switch between readings, because the resistor warms if current flows for long.

records.why: A real 9 V, 2.7 W filament bulb running at only 3 V is much cooler than at full brightness, so its resistance is lower than the 30 ohm value (which holds at full 9 V). Real series readings will therefore be a little above 0.10 A (about 0.15 A). Teachers are told what to expect so they do not think the equipment is faulty. How I checked: tungsten filament current rises roughly as V^0.6, so at one third of the rated voltage I is about (1/3)^0.6 x 0.30 A = 0.52 x 0.30 A = 0.16 A.
records.old: If readings differ slightly, say: 'Check that the ammeter is on the same scale and the connections are tight.'
records.new: If readings differ slightly, say: 'Check that the ammeter is on the same scale and the connections are tight.' Teacher note: a real filament is cooler and has lower resistance when it glows dimly, so real series readings may be higher than 0.10 A (about 0.15 A is normal). Accept this, and stress that the pattern (the same at every point) matters more than the exact number.
records.group_headline: Real filament bulbs would read about 0.15 A, not 0.10 A, in the series demo: teachers are told what to expect and why (a dim filament is cooler, so its resistance is lower).
records.reference: OpenStax, University Physics Volume 2, Chapter 9 'Current and Resistance' (temperature dependence of resistance, tungsten filament)

records.why: Learners who replace the resistor with the demo bulb at 3.0 V will not get exactly 0.10 A: a real bulb at 3.0 V is cool and passes about 0.15 A, so V/I is below 30 ohm. This is turned into a teaching point (a bulb is non-ohmic, a resistor at constant temperature is ohmic), which also covers the KICD idea of classifying ohmic and non-ohmic conductors. How I checked: 3.0 V / 0.15 A = 20 ohm, below 30 ohm.
records.old: Then they replace the resistor with the 30 Ω demo bulb, read 3.0 V and 0.10 A, and compare V/I.
records.new: Then they replace the resistor with the demo bulb, read 3.0 V and the current (about 0.10 A in our idealised data; a real bulb at 3.0 V is cool and may pass about 0.15 A, so V/I comes out below 30 Ω), and compare V/I with the constant 30 Ω of the resistor. A bulb whose V/I changes with temperature is non-ohmic.
records.reference: OpenStax, University Physics Volume 2, Chapter 9 'Current and Resistance' (temperature dependence of resistance, tungsten filament)

records.why: Knock-on of the filament note in Lesson 3: if learners read 0.15 A instead of 0.10 A, the teacher has an explanation ready.
records.old: Remind learners that meters are not perfect, so small differences like 0.09 A or 0.11 A are acceptable; discuss why.
records.new: Remind learners that meters are not perfect, so small differences like 0.09 A or 0.11 A are acceptable; discuss why. If the current is clearly higher (for example 0.15 A), explain that a dim filament is cooler and has lower resistance (Lesson 6), so real bulbs are not exactly 30 Ω.
records.reference: OpenStax, University Physics Volume 2, Chapter 9 'Current and Resistance' (temperature dependence of resistance, tungsten filament)

records.why: Not every school has three ammeters for every group. A low-cost substitute is listed: one digital multimeter on its current range, or rotating groups through two or three stations.
records.old: Roles: builder, ammeter reader, recorder, safety checker.
records.new: Roles: builder, ammeter reader, recorder, safety checker. Equipment note: if there are too few ammeters, one digital multimeter on its current range can serve each group in turn, or groups can rotate through two or three stations.

records.why: Station D used a coil of 'thin nichrome' to show resistance rising with temperature. Nichrome is chosen for heaters precisely because its resistance changes very little with temperature, so learners would see no clear drop in current. A tungsten bulb filament shows a large change. Now the 9 V, 2.7 W demo bulb is measured at 1.5 V (dim, cool) and 4.5 V (bright, hot), both safe supplies. How I checked: tungsten resistance rises strongly with temperature (hot filament at full brightness is about 10 times its cold value), so R = V/I at 4.5 V is clearly larger than at 1.5 V; nichrome's temperature coefficient is only about 0.0004 per kelvin.
records.old: STATION D (Temperature): a coil of thin nichrome or a torch bulb filament is tested briefly at low current and again after the circuit has been on a little longer so that it warms, noticing the ammeter reading drop.
records.new: STATION D (Temperature): the 9 V, 2.7 W demo bulb is connected first to one 1.5 V cell (dim and cool) and then to three cells in the holder (4.5 V, brighter and hotter). Learners record V and I each time and calculate R = V/I, and see that R is larger when the filament is hot. (Nichrome is not used here because its resistance changes too little with temperature to see on school meters; the 30 Ω value of the bulb is its resistance at full brightness on 9 V.)
records.group_headline: Temperature station used nichrome, whose resistance hardly changes with temperature, so learners would not see the effect: now a bulb filament measured dim and bright.
records.reference: OpenStax, University Physics Volume 2, Chapter 9 'Current and Resistance' (temperature dependence of resistance, tungsten filament)

records.why: Knock-on of the Station D change: the explanation now refers to R = V/I of the hot filament rather than the ammeter reading of a nichrome coil.
records.old: so the ammeter reading falls as the wire warms.
records.new: so R = V/I is larger for the hot, bright filament than for the dim one.
records.reference: OpenStax, University Physics Volume 2, Chapter 9 'Current and Resistance' (temperature dependence of resistance, tungsten filament)

records.why: Knock-on of the Station D change: the Summary Table prompt now matches what learners actually measure.
records.old: A warm metal wire let less current flow.
records.new: The bulb filament had a larger R when it was hot and bright than when it was dim.
records.reference: OpenStax, University Physics Volume 2, Chapter 9 'Current and Resistance' (temperature dependence of resistance, tungsten filament)

records.why: With a 4.5 V supply, 25 cm of nichrome of ordinary thickness would carry several amperes and heat quickly. For 0.2 mm diameter nichrome: resistance per metre = resistivity / area = 1.1e-6 / (3.14 x (1e-4)^2) = about 35 ohm per metre, so 25 cm is about 8.8 ohm and the current is 4.5 / 8.8 = 0.51 A (and 0.13 A at 100 cm), which a school ammeter can read. Teachers should check which wire gauges their school has.
records.old: nichrome wire of fixed thickness is tested at 25 cm, 50 cm, 75 cm and 100 cm.
records.new: nichrome wire of fixed thickness is tested at 25 cm, 50 cm, 75 cm and 100 cm (use thin wire of about 0.2 mm diameter, roughly 35 Ω per metre, so the current stays at or below about 0.5 A; thicker nichrome would carry several amperes from the 4.5 V supply and heat quickly).

records.why: Ordinary 5 A fuse wire needs several amperes to melt. A pack of six dry cells cannot supply that, so the demonstration as written would probably not work. A single thin strand of steel wool, the usual low-voltage demonstration, breaks at about an ampere or less. Teachers should check their own equipment before the lesson.
records.old: Mr. Otieno connects a short piece of thin fuse wire in series with a 9 V supply and a bulb bank, then increases the number of parallel bulbs (or reduces the series resistance) until the thin wire glows and melts.
records.new: Mr. Otieno connects a single thin strand of steel wool (ordinary 5 A fuse wire needs several amperes, which a dry-cell pack cannot supply) in series with a 9 V supply and a bulb bank, then increases the number of parallel bulbs until the strand glows and breaks.

records.why: 'Lesson 10 style values' was a wrong cross-reference: Lesson 10 contains no kettle or heater data. The data is now given directly and linked to the P = IV idea of Lesson 10.
records.old: use the table of appliance data from Lesson 10 style values: kettle 3000 W, heater 2000 W, mains 240 V.
records.new: use this appliance data: kettle 3000 W, heater 2000 W, mains 240 V (the same P = IV idea as Lesson 10).

records.why: The 'porter carrying energy' picture had no stated limits, although the lesson plan claimed it was 'explicitly critiqued'. A limit is added: coulombs are not used up; each returns to the battery and picks up energy again, only the energy is handed over.
records.old: Contrast: 'e.m.f. belongs to the source; p.d. belongs to the component.'
records.new: Contrast: 'e.m.f. belongs to the source; p.d. belongs to the component.' Name the limits of the porter picture: the porters (charge) are not used up, since each one returns to the battery round the loop and collects energy again, and the bulb keeps no charge; only the energy is handed over.
records.group_headline: Analogies (matatus and bucket brigade in Lesson 3, porter carrying energy in Lesson 4) had no stated limits: limits are now named for the teacher.

records.why: The matatu and bucket-brigade pictures had no stated limits. Added: charge carriers stay in the loop and are not used up, and neither picture shows the energy transferred (Lesson 4).
records.old: Link: 'A series loop has no turn-offs, so the same current passes everywhere.'
records.new: Link: 'A series loop has no turn-offs, so the same current passes everywhere.' Name the limits of both pictures: matatus are separate vehicles that can leave the road, but charge carriers stay in the loop and are never used up, and neither picture shows the energy that the bulbs transfer (Lesson 4).

records.why: The CBE level names (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches) now appear in the descriptor text, and the descriptors were rewritten so that the lowest printed level describes partial success. The old third level described work that belongs to Below Expectations (for example 'few or incorrect values'). The Below Expectations level cannot be added in the current contract (see the separate flag).

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: uses the exact values from the demos and classroom (90 Ω, 10 Ω, 0.10 A, 0.30 A, 3.0 V, 9.0 V, 0.30 W, 2.7 W, 0.15 A, 0.60 A, 0.45 A) accurately and links every one to a claim.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: uses most of the correct values and links most of them to claims; some values are missing or not clearly linked.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: uses some correct values, but several are missing or incorrect, or the claims are only partly supported by evidence.

value.criterion: Scientific reasoning about series and parallel circuits
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: clearly explains that series bulbs share the p.d. and carry a single current through 90 Ω, while parallel branches each get the full p.d. and independent currents, and links this to why one blown tube does not affect the others.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: explains the series and parallel difference correctly, with limited reasoning about p.d., current or resistance.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: describes what happens in series and parallel but gives an incomplete or partly incorrect reason (for example a hint that bulbs use up current).

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: all calculations (V = IR, resistance in series and parallel, P = IV, E = Pt, cost) are set out step by step with correct units and answers.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: calculations are mostly correct, with minor errors in units or steps.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: some calculations are correct, but several are incomplete, incorrect or missing units.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: correctly explains the fuse blowing at 20.8 A against 13 A, the roles of the fuse or breaker and earthing, and the cost saving of an LED, in Kenyan contexts.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: explains most safety and cost ideas correctly, with some gaps.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: explains some safety or cost ideas, but they are unclear or incomplete.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: compares the first model with the final model, names a specific change, links to both KICD questions, and uses scientific terms (in series, in parallel, p.d., e.m.f.) correctly.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: describes a change in the model and uses most terms correctly.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: mentions a model change only vaguely, or uses several terms incorrectly.

records.why: The partner contract allows only three rubric levels per criterion, and the printed headings are fixed by the template, so the fourth CBE level 'Below Expectations' cannot be represented. Suggestion: teachers add it by hand as 'Below Expectations: gives few or incorrect values, claims without evidence, or shows misconceptions such as bulbs using up current' (the wording of the old third level). The partner/template owner must decide whether to extend the contract.

The Final Explanation should assess whether learners can choose the right ideas to explain the phenomenon. Prompt (b) listed 'closed loops, p.d. and current', which supplies the reasoning. The other items raised by the audit were checked: Part 2(d) only repeats Wanjiru's question already in the stem, Part 3(e) asks 'Is he right?' and so does not state the answer, and Part 1(a) does not reveal 'parallel' (the stem only says the tubes share the mains), so no change was made there.
records.old: (b) Using what you learned about closed loops, p.d. and current, explain why the other three tubes are not affected.
records.new: (b) Explain why the other three tubes are not affected.
records.where: Final Explanation, Part 1: Why the other tubes stay lit, prompt

records.why: The data paraphrased the KICD outcomes and listed six (a to f); KICD lists five. Restored the KICD March 2025 wording word for word. The old outcome 'draw circuit diagrams' is not a KICD outcome for this sub-strand, but circuit symbols are still taught in Lesson 2 as the language for everything else. NOTE: KICD outcomes (a), (b) and (d) include content that this lesson sequence does not teach (see the flag on unit content).
records.old:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) draw circuit diagrams using standard circuit symbols,
b) explain the relationship between current, potential difference and resistance in a circuit,
c) investigate factors affecting the resistance of a conductor,
d) determine the effective resistance of resistors connected in series and in parallel,
e) apply Ohm's law and the relations P = IV and E = IVt to solve problems on current electricity,
f) appreciate the application of series and parallel circuits in day-to-day life and the need for electrical safety.
records.new:
By the end of the sub strand, the learner should be able to:
a) explain the terminologies used in current electricity,
b) verify the relationships: V=IR, E=I(R+r) as used in current electricity, determine the resistance and resistivity of various conductors using different methods,
c) determine effective resistance of various resistor networks,
d) determine the relationship of potential difference and current to power as used in heating effect of an electric current,
e) appreciate the applications of current electricity in day-to-day life.
records.group_headline: UNIT outcomes, content, competencies, values and PCI restored to the KICD March 2025 wording (the data had paraphrased them, and listed an extra sixth outcome).
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Physics, Strand 3.0 Electricity and Magnetism, Sub-Strand 3.2 Current Electricity

records.why: Replaced the data's own content list with the KICD content bullets word for word (KICD prints 'a.m.' in the first bullet; it is copied as written). Content that this sequence also teaches but KICD does not list is shown on a separate line so nothing is lost.

records.why: The KICD core competencies for this sub-strand are Critical thinking and problem solving, and Learning to learn, with a specific KICD sentence for each. These are restored word for word, followed by how each is met in this unit. The three extra competencies the data listed are kept, marked as additions. The 'Digital literacy: circuit simulations' line was not tied to any lesson activity, so it now refers to the linked digital resources where a device is available.
records.value:
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: the learner develops the evaluation and decision-making skill while deriving the mathematical relationship between emf, potential difference, electric current, resistance and use it to solve related problems. In this unit: the learner analyses why bulbs in series are dimmer than bulbs in parallel and why one failed tube does not switch off the others, then solves circuit problems (Lessons 5, 7 to 11).
• Learning to learn: the learner develops the skill of carrying out research while performing an experiment to investigate the relationship between potential difference and current through a conductor and draw the requisite graphs. In this unit: the learner draws the V-I graph in Lesson 5 and revises their circuit model after each investigation.
• Communication and collaboration (added for this unit): the learner works in groups to build circuits, share measurements and justify claims using evidence.
• Creativity and imagination (added for this unit): the learner designs a safe household lighting circuit for a classroom or home (Lesson 12).
• Digital literacy (added for this unit): the learner uses the linked digital resources, such as circuit simulations where a device is available, to test predictions about series and parallel circuits.
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Physics, Strand 3.0 Electricity and Magnetism, Sub-Strand 3.2 Current Electricity

records.value:

• Education for sustainable development (added for this unit): the learner explores energy saving by using efficient lighting such as LEDs and solar power in homes and schools.
• Financial literacy (added for this unit): the learner calculates the cost of electricity use (kWh) for household appliances.

records.why: The data's 'KICD key inquiry questions' were not the KICD ones. KICD's two questions for Sub-Strand 3.2 are 'How is current electricity applicable in our day-to-day life?' and 'Why are resistors used in electrical circuits?'. The data's first question was invented and the KICD question about resistors was missing. Restored word for word; every lesson's key inquiry line, the Final Explanation and the Lesson 12 board discussion are updated to match.

records.old: KICD question 1: we found the relationship by measuring V and I for the 30 Ω resistor; V/I stayed 30 Ω, so V = IR, and current rises with p.d. and falls with resistance. KICD question 2: current electricity is applied in home and school wiring, with lights in parallel, fuses or breakers on the live wire, earthing, and choosing efficient LEDs to cut the cost of energy in kWh.
records.new: KICD question 1 (how is current electricity applicable in our day-to-day life?): current electricity is applied in home and school wiring, with lights in parallel, fuses or breakers on the live wire, earthing, and choosing efficient LEDs to cut the cost of energy in kWh. KICD question 2 (why are resistors used in electrical circuits?): a resistor controls the current, because for the same p.d. a larger resistance gives a smaller current (we found V = IR by measuring V and I for the 30 Ω resistor: V/I stayed 30 Ω), and resistors in series share out the p.d. (3.0 V each across three 30 Ω bulbs); a high-resistance element also turns electrical energy into heat, as in a heater or a long thin cable (Lesson 6).

records.why: KICD content and outcomes that this 12-lesson sequence does not teach or assess: internal resistance and E = I(R + r) (outcome b); resistivity as a quantity and 'various methods' of finding resistance, including resistor colour codes, the Wheatstone bridge and the metre bridge (outcome b and content); classifying conductors as ohmic or non-ohmic (only touched on in Lesson 5); the 'applications of resistors' content beyond heater elements and fuse wire. KICD allocates 22 lessons to this sub-strand and this sequence has 12 lessons (22 periods once double lessons are counted), so no lessons can be added here. Suggestion: teachers decide whether to add short extensions (for example internal resistance in Lesson 9 with the cells, resistivity rho = RA/L in Lesson 6, colour codes as homework in Lesson 5) or accept the gap. Strand and sub-strand numbers (3.0 and 3.2) and the name 'Current Electricity' match KICD.
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Physics, Strand 3.0 Electricity and Magnetism, Sub-Strand 3.2 Current Electricity

records.why: The teacher script contained an unfinished sentence ('nine times... no, three times bigger') that would confuse a teacher. Rewritten as a clean question with the expected answer. Recomputed: current 0.30 A / 0.10 A = 3, p.d. 9.0 V / 3.0 V = 3, power 2.7 W / 0.30 W = 9 = 3 x 3.
records.old: "Why is the current in parallel nine times... no, three times bigger in each branch but nine times more power?"
records.new: "The current in each parallel branch is three times bigger (0.30 A against 0.10 A), but the power is nine times bigger. Why?" (Expected: the p.d. is also three times bigger, 9.0 V against 3.0 V, and P = IV, so 3 x 3 = 9.)

records.why: The plan says the parallel bulb is '9 times brighter'. What is 9 times larger is the POWER (2.7 W against 0.30 W). Brightness to the eye is not simply proportional to power, and a cool tungsten filament gives far less light for its power. A teacher note is added so teachers say 'nine times the power, and clearly brighter'. How I checked: 2.7 / 0.30 = 9.
records.new: so P = 0.30 W.' Teacher note: 9 times the power does not mean 9 times the brightness to the eye, so say "nine times the power, and clearly brighter", not "nine times brighter".
records.group_headline: '9 times brighter' corrected to '9 times the power': brightness is not simply proportional to power.
records.reference: Illuminating Engineering Society, IES Lighting Handbook, incandescent lamp operating characteristics (light output changes much faster than power as voltage changes)

records.why: Expected answers were missing for the 'remove bulb B' test, which learners are asked to predict. Added. Recomputed: with B removed only A and C remain in series, 30 + 30 = 60 ohm, I = 9 / 60 = 0.15 A; each has 4.5 V, so P = 4.5 x 0.15 = 0.675 W for each. Before: A had 6.0 V x 0.20 A = 1.2 W and C had 3.0 V x 0.10 A = 0.30 W, so A becomes dimmer and C brighter.
records.old: They then unscrew bulb B and observe that C stays lit but A changes (the current falls).
records.new: They then unscrew bulb B and observe that C stays lit and glows brighter while A glows dimmer (expected: the ammeter falls to 0.15 A, because only A and C remain in series, 30 + 30 = 60 Ω and 9/60 = 0.15 A; each now has 4.5 V).
